tagline: A mountain crossing from Castle Gate’s coal country to the Uintah Basin.
intro: US 191 links Helper and Duchesne through steep rock formations and stands of conifer and aspen, approaching the 10,000-foot level at Indian Summit. Indian Canyon is a state scenic byway within the Dinosaur Diamond Prehistoric Highway National Scenic Byway. The Forest Service highlights its changing rock and forest landscapes between the San Rafael Swell and Uintah Basin.

The connection entered Utah’s state highway system in 1910, when it ran from Colton to Duchesne. Its southwest end shifted to Castle Gate in 1912, and the road became State Route 33 in 1927. Few roadway changes followed before US 191 absorbed it in 1981. By then Castle Gate’s residents had been relocated, and coal-loading facilities had replaced the townsite. That renumbering was part of a much larger extension: Utah’s Department of Transportation joined Montana, Wyoming and Arizona in seeking a new US 191 alignment that absorbed several state routes.

From the Castle Gate end, the US 191 corridor follows Willow Creek beside the western beginning of the Roan Cliffs. Beyond the high crossing at Indian Summit, the road reaches Duchesne and its junction with US 40. The town lies just west of the meeting of the Strawberry and Duchesne rivers. Cottonwoods and willows line the river banks at Duchesne.

moments.title: Castle Gate
moments.text: Castle Gate takes its name from two sheer sandstone walls beside the Price River near the mouth of Price Canyon. The town’s first coal mine opened around 1886 after the railroad arrived, supplying coal for steam trains. Railroad demand shaped the mining settlement: the Utah Fuel Company and the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad owned and tightly controlled the town. In 1924, explosions killed all 171 men working in Mine No. 2; a rescue crew leader also died. The town was dismantled in 1974, its residents moved to a subdivision west of Helper, and the site cleared for coal-loading facilities.

moments.title: Roan Cliffs
moments.text: The Roan Cliffs begin beside Willow Creek and the US 191 corridor, on the southern edge of the West Tavaputs Plateau. They extend nearly 190 miles into Colorado, above and north of the separate Book Cliffs. The Book Cliffs name is also applied to both landforms, obscuring the distinction. John Wesley Powell called these the Brown Cliffs; their official name changed to Roan Cliffs in 1932 to match their color. Eastward, the Green River cuts through them in Desolation and Gray canyons. The cliffs then continue along the southern edge of the East Tavaputs Plateau, extending the landform far beyond this road crossing.

moments.title: Duchesne
moments.text: At Duchesne, two rivers meet: the Strawberry drains the eastern Wasatch slopes, while the Duchesne drains the southwest side of the Uinta Mountains. Crossing the Strawberry at Indian Canyon once required a local building effort. The town’s Boosters Club raised $500 for a bridge completed in 1908; the state replaced it in 1914. The joined waters continue east as the Duchesne River to the Green River at Ouray. Cottonwoods and willows grow along the banks, while sagebrush and rabbitbrush occupy unirrigated bench tops. The town sits at the junction of US 191, US 40 and State Route 87.
